text: Hundreds of teens have returned alone to New Orleans to finish high school with friends. For parents that can be a scary decision, and school officials say they lack of supervision is causing problems.
Katia Dunn reports.

It's Friday at Edna Karr High School in the Algiers neighborhood, and the administration has organized a volleyball game: faculty versus students. The students are winning. Senior Alvin Davis has appointed himself coach of the student's team.

speaker_label: Mr. ALVIN DAVIS (Senior, Edna Karr High School)
text: If they score again, you're going to get in, you're going to get in, and you're going to get in.

Davis is 18, but he's such a natural leader, he can pass himself off as the actual coach. Part of the reason he's so at ease is that he's been going to school with these kids since he was in seventh-grade.

resolved_label: Mr. ALVIN DAVIS (Senior, Edna Karr High School)
text: You can't trade in friends you've been having since, you know, knee-high for anybody else or anywhere else. So I will not go to any other high school. I refuse to graduate from anywhere else. So since it's something I want that bad, I'm going to do pretty much whatever it takes to be happy.

One thing it took was, as he put it, begging and acting depressed until his parents agreed to let him come back without them. In August, he moved into a crowded FEMA trailer with his best friend, Jeremiah, and his family. After the storm, Davis and his family moved a couple times, first to Arkansas and then to Baker, Louisiana. He tried new schools and didn't like them.

He's lucky that his parents are only an hour and a half away now. He's able to go home often on weekends. He says they were reluctant to let him go, but they knew how important it was to him to finish high school with his friends.
Davis isn't the only teenager in this situation. School officials estimate there are 75 of them in this high school and hundreds across the city. Erica Boyd is also a senior at Karr.

speaker_label: Ms. ERICA BOYD (Senior, Edna Karr High School)
text: I've was used to wearing a uniform. So every school in Houston didn't have uniforms so you had to buy clothes to wear to school, or whatever. So they would wear heels and skirts. It's just school, like that's not us.

Like Davis, Boyd lives with her best friend's family now. Other students have moved in with relatives, and some - no one knows how many - are living in the city unsupervised. Not all students are handling independence as well as Davis and Boyd seem to be. School officials say there are more fights. Discipline is a huge problem; teachers can spend way too much time dealing with kids who are talking back or refusing to heed authority.

speaker_label: Mr. DAVID GRUBB (Director of Communications, Algiers Charter Schools Association)
text: They don't really have someone at home to either set their boundaries, or reinforce what's going on in the schools.

David Grubb is the director of communications for Algiers Charter School Association. He says there are also legal issues. Administrators don't know who to call in emergencies, or for questions about medical history. No one can sign registrations forms. Parent/teacher conferences or signatures on report cards are suddenly huge obstacles.
Edna Metcalf is a social worker at the school. She says, in addition to the challenges of the living independently, many of these students are still dealing with the emotional aftermath of the storm.

speaker_label: Ms. EDNA METCALF (Social Worker, Edna Karr High School)
text: The kids are just -they're just in so much need of help. I mean they really are. I say it all the time, I could use five full-time social workers here. I mean, easily.

The separation takes its toll on parents too. I called Erica Boyd's mom, Tammy Hawkins, who's now in Georgia. She said she agonized over the decision to let Erica go, but Hawkins thought it would be easier than watching her daughter moping around every day.
I knew it was really important to her because of her personality, the kind of child she is. She doesn't adjust well to new environments.
still, Hawkins feels like she's missing out on too big a part of her daughter's life. And if she had to do it over again, she says, she wouldn't let Erica go.
Katia Dunn, NPR News, New Orleans.
This is NPR News.

From NPR News, it's Day to Day. The economy is doing so badly now that the number of new homes being built fell nearly 20 percent last month, and that is the biggest decline in a generation. Nevada used to see new homes going up every day. Now, it has the nation's highest foreclosure rate. Producer Katia Dunn was in Nevada recently. She says it reminded her of another disaster she covered.

A few months ago, I covered Hurricanes Ike and Gustav. One thing I noticed about reporting a natural disaster: I felt like I should interview literally everyone I ran into on the street. Everyone's life was touched by the hurricane. I had the same feeling reporting on the housing crisis in Las Vegas. Nearly half the homes there are under water, meaning homeowners owe more on their houses than they're worth. If the people we met weren't in danger of losing their own house, they were involved in other ways. In fact, it was so easy to find people caught up in the housing crisis, at one point, we simply walked up and down the street, knocking on doors and talking to people. But there is one giant difference between people who are living through a financial disaster and those who are living through a natural one.
Ms. DEANA O'REEHR (Loan Consultant, Las Vegas, Nevada): People do not want to talk about it. They do not want to talk about their situation at all.

Deana O'Reehr(ph) is a loan consultant. She helps people in foreclosure. Often when people run into trouble, she says, their instinct is to hide. They don't want to confess that they didn't make their payments or made a bad investment. O'Reehr is also fighting to keep her own home. She says the company unlawfully took over her property, and it helped, she says, when she tells people they're not alone.

Ms. O'REEHR: I basically, immediately, tell them my story. I say, you know what? I'm there. I've been there for year. I owe so much money, it's not even funny. I just tell them my realness, and then they usually will open up.

speaker_label: Mr. ISRAEL TWILLY (Resident, Las Vegas, Nevada)
text: It's embarrassing, too. It's really embarrassing.

That was Israel Twilly(ph). He moved to Las Vegas a few years ago to retire. He and his wife are now under water on their house and struggling to make the payments. He's gone back to work. He explained to us that one of the hardest parts of this situation is just admitting it, even to his family.

speaker_label: Mr. ISRAEL TWILLY (Resident, Las Vegas, Nevada)
text: Because when you've got grandkids that depend on you, they always want Grandma and Granddad to bring around Christmas presents, and the kids, you know, they expect - even though they're grown, they still expect Christmas presents. So, it's embarrassing, you know, not to be able to do it.
I worked with reporter Yuki Noguchi on this story. She thinks that another reason people can't quite bring themselves to face this problem is that it's not over.

I don't think it's that people aren't willing to talk; I don't think they know who to talk to. And you know, a lot of them just are fearful of hopelessness. You know, they're afraid that if they reach out and talk to somebody, that they're going to be told they're going to lose their home. And so, they'd rather just hunker down and hope for the best.

After a real natural disaster hits, people start putting their lives back together. In Las Vegas, people wake up and face a crisis every day. It's not exactly like a financial hurricane passed through this city. It's more like hurricane season is just getting started. Katia Dunn, NPR News.
Stay with us. Day to Day returns in a moment.

When General Electric was born more than a century ago, it went on to become one of many companies with names that implied universal appeal and consistency, think Standard Oil, General Tire. Now with General Motors and General Electric facing hard times, our generals are in retreat. Here's NPR's Katia Dunn.
In the mid-1980's General Motors ran a commercial showing a generic-looking salesman slashing prices.
Nobody but General Motors offers so many deals on so many cars for so many people.
The message in this ad is simple. General Motors has all types of cars and lots of people to buy them. At the time, that was a standard sales technique.
Unidentified Man #1: Standard Oil. More new car owners in the Midwest use our lead-free Amoco than any other brand.
That ad ran in 1976 for Standard Oil.
MR. ROBERT PASKOFF (Brand Keys): And that's a commodity. That's not a brand.

Robert Paskoff is president of Brand Keys. He says when these early large companies were building their reputations, they used the terms standard and general. It was simply the best way to introduce consumers to the products they wanted to buy for a good price. But in the late part of the 20th century, the ads all started to sound alike.
By 1985, everyone was pretty much doing everything the same way.

Companies needed to distinguish themselves from their many competitors, plus consumers were starting to control the information that came to them. They flipped the channels, they tuned out. If they didn't like the product, they didn't use it. Today, Paskoff says, rational name recognition is simply not enough to make the sale.
If I say General Motors to you, you'd probably go, uh, and that uh is the sound of a brand that's dying.

Now consultants say companies want consumers to form emotional relationships with brands. That leaves more to the imagination. And it's easier to do with mysterious names. Standard Oil of New Jersey becomes Exxon; part of AT&T became Verizon. Of course some companies have adopted these meaningless names in an effort to break up with consumers and start over.
Unidentified Man #2: Give me a cigarette, will you, huh?
Don't say cigarette, say Phillip Morris.
Unidentified Man #2: Oh? Is there any other kind?

In 2007, Philip Morris became Altria. Just last month the contractor Blackwater changed its name. The company got a lot of bad press after the Iraqi government expelled it. It's new name? Xe, spelled X-E.
Katia Dunn, NPR News, Washington.
Our brand is the same. It's NPR News.
